## The problem

We want to predict a county's monthly **satellite-detected burned-area fraction**, up to
twelve months ahead. The intended panel has 3,108 continental US counties and 264 months,
January 2003 through December 2024. Detected burning includes prescribed and agricultural
fire as well as wildfire, so this response should not be called wildfire risk.

The response mixes exact zeros with positive fractions. We use a hurdle Beta model and
compare two ways to estimate it: [gradient-boosted trees](xgboostlss.qmd) and a
[graph-convolutional LSTM](pytorch.qmd). Both use information available at the forecast origin.

The tutorial follows the modelling workflow: define the information available to a
forecast, fit on train, tune on test, examine train/test residuals, then assess the chosen
class representatives on validation.

After the two model chapters, [Comparison](comparison.qmd) brings together the
train/test evidence. [Discussion](discussion.qmd) then assesses the fixed fits on
validation.

## What a forecast may know {#sec-tracks}

Let $y_{ct}$ be the detected burned fraction for county $c$ in month $t$. A forecast
issued from origin $o$ predicts $y_{c,o+h}$ for horizons $h=1,\ldots,12$.

Both models receive fixed terrain, calendar features, county geography, and historical
burned fractions. Terrain is frozen from the first training month. Every response-history
index is between zero and the origin. Annual land cover, population, built area, fuel
cover, and target-month weather, drought, vegetation, and snow are excluded. The
categorical land-cover input is also removed.

These are **retrospective rolling-origin forecasts**: historical observations through the
stated origin are assumed available. Later origins can use observations that occurred
since earlier forecasts were made, including past observations from an earlier split.
No response after the origin enters a forecast's inputs; training targets enter the
fitting loss in the usual supervised-learning role. Operational product-release delays are not
modelled here.

The [data chapter](data.qmd) describes the checks behind this information set.

## The hurdle Beta likelihood {#sec-likelihood}

Write $\pi$ for the probability that the detected fraction is zero. Given a positive
response, use a Beta distribution with mean $\mu$ and precision $\phi$:

$$
\Pr(Y=0)=\pi,\qquad
Y\mid Y>0\sim\mathrm{Beta}(\alpha,\beta),\qquad
\alpha=\mu\phi,\quad\beta=(1-\mu)\phi.
$$ {#eq-meanprec}

Here $0<\pi<1$, $0<\mu<1$, and $\phi>0$. The positive component has

$$
E[Y\mid Y>0]=\mu,\qquad
\mathrm{Var}(Y\mid Y>0)=\frac{\mu(1-\mu)}{1+\phi}.
$$

The unconditional expected fraction combines occurrence and magnitude:

$$
E[Y]=(1-\pi)\mu.
$$ {#eq-ey}

The prediction files call $1-\pi$ `p_occ` and the product `e_y`.
These are distinct summaries: a model can rank occurrence well while misestimating
positive magnitudes. “Occurrence” here means positive satellite detection, not an
independently verified physical ignition.

The hurdle likelihood separates the zero mass from the continuous density:

$$
\log p(y)=
\begin{cases}
\log\pi,&y=0,\\
\log(1-\pi)+\log f_{\mathrm{Beta}}(y;\mu\phi,(1-\mu)\phi),&0<y<1.
\end{cases}
$$ {#eq-loglik}

The negative average of these contributions is **NLL**, the fitting and tuning objective.
Lower is better. A density can exceed one, so a negative NLL is possible. Summing these
marginal scores over correlated county-months does not make those observations independent.

### Handling zero without moving positive observations

The Beta density must not score the zero atom. Numerical evaluation also needs to keep
the unused branch finite: passing zero to a logarithm can poison automatic differentiation
even when the resulting branch is discarded.

```python
is_positive = y > 0
y_for_beta = torch.where(is_positive, y, torch.full_like(y, 0.5))
log_beta = torch.distributions.Beta(mu * phi, (1 - mu) * phi).log_prob(y_for_beta)
log_prob = torch.where(
    is_positive,
    torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(-zero_logit) + log_beta,
    torch.nn.functional.logsigmoid(zero_logit),
)
loss = -log_prob.mean()
```

The dummy 0.5 affects only a discarded calculation for zero rows. Every positive response
is scored at its observed value; it is not clamped upward to an epsilon. The maximum
training-set burned fraction is **0.5641801116** (about **56.42%**), observed in
Clark County, Kansas (FIPS 20025), in March 2017. It is well below one, so the
training responses do not require a probability mass at that endpoint.

## Fitting, tuning, and assessment {#sec-protocol}

The repository's split names have the following roles:

| Split | Assigned panel months | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Train | January 2003–May 2018 | Fit parameters and preprocessing; inspect residuals |
| Test | June 2018–July 2020 | Tune hyperparameters and checkpoints; compare performance and residuals |
| Validation | August 2020–December 2024 | Assess the two selected class representatives |

The models share a 48-month lookback and twelve-month target horizon. A window belongs
to a split only when its entire target horizon falls within that split. Training-history
overlap across windows is permitted; assigning the same response target to different
splits is not.

The initial 48 months provide encoder/history warmup, so scored training targets
begin in January 2007 rather than at the start of the training panel.

Each class is tuned by minimizing the hurdle Beta NLL with the stated forecast inputs.
The representative is the finite, completed trial with the lowest test NLL; pruned or failed
trials cannot become the selected fit. Train/test diagnostics explain the strengths and
limitations of that representative. Both model examples remain in the tutorial without
requiring a definitive class winner.

Validation is evaluated after the architecture, hyperparameters, and checkpoints are
fixed. It assesses the selected representatives on a later target period.

## Reading the scores and diagnostics

NLL assesses the predicted zero mass and positive density. We also report the
**continuous ranked probability score** (CRPS), which compares the predictive CDF $F$
to the observation:

$$
\mathrm{CRPS}(F,y)=E|X-y|-\tfrac12E|X-X'|,\qquad X,X'\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}F.
$$ {#eq-crps-kernel}

For the hurdle Beta, this expectation has a closed form. Write $q=1-\pi$,
$a=\mu\phi$, $b=(1-\mu)\phi$, let $B(a,b)$ be the Beta function, and let
$I_y(a,b)$ be the regularized incomplete Beta function (the Beta CDF).
For $0\leq y\leq1$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathrm{CRPS}(F,y)
={}&\pi y+q\left[y\{2I_y(a,b)-1\}
       +\mu\{1-2I_y(a+1,b)\}\right]\\
 &-\pi q\mu
 -\frac{2q^2}{a+b}\frac{B(2a,2b)}{B(a,b)^2}.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-crps-hurdle-beta}

The first line is $E|X-y|$. The second subtracts half the expected distance
between two independent predictions, including the zero–positive pairs.
The formula also applies at an observed zero, with $I_0(a,b)=0$; it needs
neither simulated draws nor a displacement of the response.

CRPS is in burned-fraction units, and lower is better. NLL and CRPS emphasize different
properties, so a model can improve one more than the other. Occurrence AUC/AP, the Brier
score, and errors in the expected fraction add interpretable views of performance.

For the residual diagnostics, randomize the PIT within the CDF jump at zero and transform
it to a normal quantile: $U\sim\mathrm{Uniform}(F(y^-),F(y))$ and $r=\Phi^{-1}(U)$.
A correctly specified known marginal gives a marginal standard-normal residual.
It does not create independence across counties, months, or repeated horizons.

Use QQ plots, occurrence reliability, and temporal/spatial residual structure to see what
a mean score hides. The plots are descriptive; millions of overlapping county-horizon rows
are not millions of independent replications.
